description: I AM A CSE(DS) STUDENT AT SRMIST WITH SKILLS IN AI,BACKEND,DATA STRUCTURES LOOKING FOR PEOPLE GOOD AT FRONTEND AND DATA WORK
summary: Case Files is an AI detective for Earth's trends. Pick a variable (air temperature, rainfall, night ground temperature or greenness) and a place, and it tells you what is changing, where, how much, and whether the change is significant or could be chance. Each investigation is a solved case: one plain question, evidence from NASA satellite and climate data, the other explanations it checked, the strongest argument against its own conclusion, and an honest verdict: strong, moderate or inconclusive. A tested statistics pipeline computes every number; AI only writes the plain-English narration, and a guard rejects any figure that isn't in the data. Our first cases cover Chennai and the Nilgiris in India, from 45 years of NASA weather records to 26 years of MODIS satellite pixels. It matters because people can see which local changes are real and which aren't yet, with every number traceable to a NASA dataset.
details:
What it does. Earth-data tools show charts and leave the hard part, deciding what is real, to the reader. Case Files does the deciding, honestly. You pick a variable and a place; it answers four questions from the challenge: what is changing, where, how much, and whether the change is significant. Each finding is presented as a detective's case file in five parts: the question, the evidence, the other suspects it checked, a Devil's Advocate objection against its own finding, and a verdict labelled strong, moderate or inconclusive. An inconclusive verdict is treated as a finding, not a failure.

Explore: select any variable. The Explore page lists 9 variables (air temperature, very hot days, heavy-rain days, wettest day, yearly rainfall, night ground temperature, greenness, and two city-minus-countryside gaps) at 11 places. For the chosen variable it ranks every place from the fastest rise to the fastest fall on one axis, so you can see the same variable moving in opposite directions in different places, then shows the trend chart and the verdict for the place you pick.

What our first cases found.

  • Chennai's nights are warming at all four city points, by +0.38 to +0.69 °C per decade over 2000–2025 (strong). The three farmland controls warmed too, by +0.27 to +0.57 °C per decade, so the city-minus-countryside gap shows no clear trend yet: a lead, not a finding. NASA's Terra and Aqua satellites agree on the direction at every point.
  • Greenness moves both ways: the OMR IT corridor is browning (−0.040 NDVI per decade, moderate) and so is the Ooty pixel in the Nilgiris (−0.028, strong), while several farmland points are greening.
  • Chennai's air temperature trend since 1981 (+0.065 °C per decade) does not clear the bar, while the whole planet's (+0.211) clearly does. We say so rather than overstate it.
  • Detector check: the 2015 Chennai floods come out as the wettest November–December in 45 years (1,267.9 mm).

How it works. A Python pipeline downloads NASA data once, removes the seasons, and tests each record with the Mann-Kendall test using a moving-block bootstrap p-value (which stays honest on autocorrelated climate data), plus Sen's slope for the size of the trend. All 40 regional tests sit in one Benjamini-Hochberg false-discovery family, frozen in advance; 18 pass. Countryside references must be MODIS cropland in both 2001 and 2024. Synthetic-data tests check that the detector finds planted trends and rarely raises false alarms on noise. A language model then writes the plain-English narration from the case file only, and a number guard rejects any figure that isn't in it. Every statistical choice is explained on the site's Method page, where judges can shuffle a real record, see all 40 tests against the false-discovery bar, and check which spots qualify as countryside.

Benefits and intended impact. City planners, journalists, students and residents can see which local changes are clear and which are not yet, with every number traceable to a NASA dataset. The same pipeline runs for any point on Earth; next we will validate against published Chennai studies and add more places and local-language narration.

Tools and languages. Python (pandas, NumPy, SciPy, pymannkendall, ruptures, pytest); TypeScript with Next.js, React, three.js / React Three Fiber, Tailwind CSS and Vitest; NASA AppEEARS for satellite data; hosted on Vercel. The site is static, so it works offline and needs no API keys. Code: github.com/Ommps246/spacejammers-casefiles (Apache 2.0).

What was built when. Before the event we built the statistics pipeline, the first seven cases and the website. During the hackathon (14–15 November) we built the Explore tool, the credits and licence, the demo video, the slide deck and this submission.

Use of AI. We took assistance from Claude Code, which generated much of the code from prompts we wrote; we reviewed, edited and tested it. The case narration is written by Claude from the case files only and checked by the number guard; AI never computes a statistic. The demo video's edit and music were made with AI assistance and are labelled in the video.
dataRefs: NASA POWER daily point data (Langley Research Center): air temperature and rainfall, 1981–2025
GISTEMP v4 global temperature record (NASA Goddard Institute for Space Studies)
MODIS MOD11A2 v6.1: Terra land surface temperature, 8-day, 1 km
MODIS MYD11A2 v6.1: Aqua land surface temperature, 8-day, 1 km
MODIS MOD13Q1 v6.1: Terra vegetation index (NDVI), 16-day, 250 m
MODIS MCD12Q1 v6.1: land cover type, yearly, 500 m
NASA AppEEARS (LP DAAC): used to extract the MODIS pixels
NASA 3D Resources: Terra satellite model (NASA/Christian A. Lopez)
NASA 3D Resources: Aqua (A) satellite model (NASA/Kevin K. Lane)
NASA Terra mission facts (overpass times, instruments)
NASA Blue Marble Earth image (NASA Visible Earth), used on the 3D globe
projectRefs: Full credits: method references (Mann 1945; Kendall 1975; Sen 1968; Kundzewicz & Robson 2004; Önöz & Bayazit 2012; Pettitt 1979; Killick et al. 2012; Benjamini & Hochberg 1995; Lenssen et al. 2019) and software
India Meteorological Department: heavy-rain threshold (64.5 mm a day)
three-globe example images (copy of NASA Blue Marble used on the globe)
Claude Code (AI coding assistance) and Claude (narration, design mockups, demo video and music)
